args.text:
Nine men's morris strategy (team X, first draft).

Placement phase:
- Take mill-capable junction points first: 5, 11, 14, 20 (4-neighbour nodes), then 2, 10, 15, 23, 8, 12, 13, 17.
- Always check first: (1) can I close a mill now? (2) must I block an opponent two-in-a-row on a line? (3) can I create a double threat (two open lines needing one piece each)?
- Avoid placing a piece where it can be boxed in with no free neighbours.

Removal choice after our mill:
- Remove an opponent piece that is part of a two-in-a-row threat or a mobile junction piece; pieces inside opponent mills are immune unless all are in mills.

Movement phase:
- Keep at least one "shuttle": a piece that can step between two points, forming a mill repeatedly (open-and-close mill). Look for moves that open a mill and threaten to re-close next turn.
- Block opponent's open-mill squares by moving a piece into the gap when they are about to close.
- Count mobility: avoid positions where our side has few legal moves (losing by no legal move is possible).
- With 3 pieces left, we can fly; keep 3 pieces able to form a line with a flying threat.

Draw awareness: 40 turns without a mill after placement = draw. If behind, aim for repetition or a draw; if ahead, force mills quickly.

args.text:
Core principles (nine men's morris, 24 points, 3 squares):
1. Placement phase: take junction points with 4 neighbours (5, 11, 14, 20) early; they give mobility and mill options on two lines each.
2. Always check first: (a) can we close a mill this turn? (b) does the opponent have two on a line with the third point free? If so, block it unless we mill first.
3. Avoid placing pieces that become immobile (corners with 2 neighbours surrounded by enemies) unless they make a threat.
4. When we close a mill, remove an opponent piece not in a mill, preferring one that is part of an opponent two-in-a-row (kills their threat) or one with high mobility.
5. Movement phase: keep pieces able to shuttle between a mill and an open point ("running mill"). Avoid moves that let the opponent slide into our mill gap.
6. Watch the 40-turn no-mill draw rule once all pieces are placed; if behind, force trades that open play; if ahead, avoid repetition and trade down.
7. With 3 pieces left we can jump anywhere: look for double threats then.
8. Use viewBoard's legal move list to confirm move numbers (move = point to place, from*100+to to move, then point to remove after a mill).
Record each game: which opening worked, whether we were first or second to move, and what the opponent tended to do.

Placement phase (worked well):
- Open 5 (junction). Then make forcing two-in-a-rows (5-8, 8-9, 9-13) that O must block, and each forced block gives us tempo.
- Before each placement check: can I close a mill? must I block O's two-in-a-row (O pieces on a line with an empty third)? does O have a point lying on two of its half-lines (a fork square like 16 here)? Take the fork square first.
- Result after placement: X on 3,5,8,9,13,16,21,22,12,20,17,23 style structure; the bottom-right/right cluster (17,20,23) was the winning mill.

Movement phase (worked well):
- Build a mill on 17-20-23 and cycle it: open by stepping a piece out (23->22 or 20->21) when no O piece is adjacent to the vacated point, then step back to re-close. O could not block because it had no piece next to 23 or 20. Check adjacency before every open: choose the open square so that the vacated point has no O neighbour.
- Do not open by moving the piece next to an O piece that can slide into the gap (e.g. 23->24 when O sat on 22).

- Removal: prefer O's most mobile piece or the piece on an open line with another O piece. Keep O's stuck pieces (blocked on all sides) unless they form a line threat.
- Once O has 3 pieces it flies: it can block any gap, so simple open/close fails. Look instead for a double threat or an existing two-in-row with an empty third that one of our pieces can slide into (game 1 winner: 9-13 with 18 empty, 17 slid to 18). Scan all lines containing two X and an empty third each turn.

Game record: Game 1, we were second to move (O). We lost: X milled in the movement phase and cut us to 2 pieces after 45 turns. The placement phase went level (9 v 9), but the movement phase was lost.

What went wrong:

Rules going forward:
1. Placement: before every placement, count the free neighbours of each of our pieces after the move. Prefer points that keep at least 2 of our pieces mobile. Do not place forcing threats whose only block gives X a useful piece unless it also leaves us mobile.
2. Keep one or two pieces in the centre ring (5, 8, 13, 20, 11, 14) even at the cost of a threat; they are the movers.
3. Before the last 3-4 placements, check the final layout: which of our pieces can move, and which X pieces can move. Aim to leave X with few legal moves (a blocked X is a win threat).
4. Movement: prefer moves that open a line for a future mill with a reachable third point (e.g. 4-11-19 needs a piece routed to 19 via 20). Avoid moving a piece that is blocking an X line.
5. Always check X's two-in-rows with an open third before each move, and keep a block ready.
6. When we mill, remove an X piece that is mobile or part of an X two-in-row.
7. The 40-turn draw rule: if level, a draw is fine; if behind on mobility, force trades.
8. With 3 pieces left we can jump anywhere; look for double threats then.
9. Confirm move numbers with the legal move list (place = point; move = from*100+to; removal = point).

Opponent (X) tendencies: blocks every single threat immediately; builds on the opposite side of our pieces; keeps centre pieces (5, 8, 9, 13) and uses 16/21/22 as movers.

args.text: Retro game 2 (draw by repetition, 53 turns). Lessons: O took 5 first so our open-5 idea was gone. Placement: my 8/9/13 pieces got boxed in by O's 5,7,14,18, and O got two fork squares (6 and 16) that I could not stop; O milled on 4-5-6 and removed my blockers on 21 twice. Movement: our pieces were frozen (only one legal move most turns), O's 4-5-6 mill was locked, so no mills and a draw. Proposal: keep mobility, avoid clusters where our own pieces block each other, and keep one free line ready for a forcing two.

Nine men's morris strategy (team X), v3 after game 2 (draw by repetition, 53 turns; game 1 won 9 vs 2).

Opponent (O) habits: opened on 5 when it moved first. Blocks direct two-in-a-rows (but not always at once). Builds two-in-rows through its own pieces, and it does find forks (game 2: 6 and 16 were double-threat squares). Slow and shuffling in movement; it does not foresee open-and-close mill cycles.

Placement:
- If 5 is free and we move first, open 5. If O holds 5, take a square on a free line through 8 or 13 (not on O's lines) and build pairs on lines with no O piece.
- Every turn, before anything else, list O's fork squares: a free point lying on two lines that each already hold one O piece and no X piece. Take the fork square or make a forcing two first. Game 2 lesson: O got 6 and 16 as forks, and we could not force, so O got a mill.
- Avoid placing pieces where they only block their own lines (8, 9, 13, 16 boxed in game 2). Prefer squares with at least 2 free neighbours and a free line.
- Keep a forcing two available for the last placements. Each two must have an empty third that O must block.
- When O has a one-move mill and we must block, block on the square that also gives us mobility (game 2: 21 was removed twice; blocking again is forced but expect it).

Movement:
- Mobility is the real goal. Count our legal moves each turn. If we have one or two, we are about to be locked; reposition early.
- Keep the 17-20-23 / 20-21 / 23-22 cycle in mind only when all the neighbours are free. Open by stepping to a square where O cannot slide into the vacated point.
- Watch O's open-and-close mill (e.g. O 5->2 then 2->5). Answer by sliding a neighbour into the gap (8->5) when we have one.
- Each turn order: (a) our one-move mill, (b) O's one-move mill (O two + empty third reachable), (c) our double threat, (d) keep our own mobility.
- Draw counter: 40 turns without a mill once placed. In game 2 we shuffled 40+ turns. If no mill is coming, change structure (open a new line) before the counter reaches 30.
- Once O has 3 pieces it flies: look for a line with two X and an empty third that we can reach.

Core principles (nine men's morris). Version 3.

Record: Game 1 lost (X milled in movement). Game 2 draw by repetition at turn 53, we were up 9 v 8 after one mill (4-5-6).

What worked (game 2):
- Open on centre-ring points 5 and 14 (4 neighbours each). X took 8 and 9, which forced blocks at 7 and 18. Those blocks were fine.
- Double threat: with 5 and 14 mine, placing 6 threatened 4 (4-5-6) and 21 (6-14-21). X could block only one. Look for a point that sits on two of my lines like this.
- After a mill, remove the X piece that blocks one of my lines (we removed 21, which reopened 6-14-21 and forced X to re-block).
- Movement squeeze: X's pieces got boxed by my blockers (5, 7, 11, 14, 18, 20). Before each move, list X's legal moves. Pick a move that frees the fewest X squares (ideally 0 or 1 X move).

What failed:
- In movement we could not convert the extra piece. A running mill (5 out to 2 and back to re-form 4-5-6) fails because X8 enters 5. One roamer alone cannot stalemate a roamer; stalemate needs 2 blockers around it. We chased X's roamer around the outer ring 3-2-1-10-22-23-24-15 for ~30 turns; repetition ended it.

Rules for next game:
1. Placement: keep 5 and 14 (or the equivalent centre points). Look for double threats before blocking-type placements.
2. Before the last placements, leave X with at most one or two mobile pieces, and keep at least 2 of our own spare movers on the outer ring (1/2/3, 10, 22/23/24, 15) so a stalemate needs only them.
3. In movement, prefer moves that give X zero or one legal reply. Count X's legal moves after each candidate.
4. Keep blockers in place: 5 (vs 8), 7 and 11 (vs 12), 14 (vs 13, 21), 18 (vs 13, 17), 20 (vs 17, 21). Do not move them unless X has no other option.
5. To win, we need a second mill line, not just stalemate. Try to bring a second piece into the ring area while X's roamer is stuck, then make a 3-in-line on the outer ring (1-2-3, 22-23-24, 3-15-24, 1-10-22).
6. Against repetition: if position repeats and we are ahead, change the plan (e.g. move a different spare piece) before 40 turns without a mill.
7. Always check X two-in-rows with an open third and block at once.
8. Use legal-move numbers: place = point; move = from*100+to; removal = point.

Opponent X: blocks every single threat at once; builds opposite our pieces; keeps one roamer on the outer ring.
